title: The Prophecy Jude Quoted
subtitle: Jude 14–15 · 1 Enoch 1:9
summary: A source-anchored comparison of the one place the New Testament quotes 1 Enoch: Jude attributes a judgment prophecy to 'Enoch, the seventh from Adam,' and the wording runs alongside 1 Enoch 1:9 in Charles' translation.

contextGuard.misuseNotice: Jude's citation of 1 Enoch is often used as a polemical weapon in canon debates — in both directions. This matrix maps the textual relationship and the distinct reception histories; it does not adjudicate which canon is correct.

edges.basisNote: Scholarly consensus holds that Jude 14–15 quotes 1 Enoch 1:9 (in the Ethiopic numbering; the passage also stands in the Greek Enoch tradition Jude's readers knew). The correspondence in wording — the coming with ten thousands of holy ones, judgment, conviction of the ungodly in deed and word — is too close to be independent.

receptionClaims.subject: 1 Enoch as Canonical Scripture
receptionClaims.text: The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church includes 1 Enoch in its Old Testament canon; it is the only church to preserve the complete text, in Ge'ez. For Tewahedo readers, Jude's citation is canon quoting canon.

sources.label: Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church canon (81 books)

receptionClaims.limit: The narrower and broader Tewahedo canon lists differ in count; 1 Enoch belongs to both.

receptionClaims.subject: Quoted but Not Canonical in Most Western Churches
receptionClaims.text: Most Western churches do not include 1 Enoch in their canon, yet the New Testament quotes it. Interpretations range from reading Jude as endorsing Enochic prophecy to reading the citation as use of a known, authoritative-in-part Second Temple work without full canonical endorsement.

sources.label: Carson & Moo, *An Introduction to the New Testament* (2005)

receptionClaims.limit: The range of positions is genuine; this matrix does not adjudicate them.

receptionClaims.subject: Enochic Literature in Second Temple Judaism
receptionClaims.text: Multiple Aramaic manuscripts of 1 Enoch were copied at Qumran, showing the work's authority in at least one Second Temple Jewish community; the rabbinic canon does not include it.
receptionClaims.limit: Qumran's practice does not generalize to all Second Temple Judaism.
